editorial.headline: Government Film and Video Production: Closed to Foreign Ownership
editorial.standfirst: A government-managed screen-production activity spanning film, video and television work, open across business scales but closed to foreign ownership nationally and in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali entry is marked **TERTUTUP**, and the national position is equally clear: foreign ownership is closed, with a ceiling of **0%**. That makes the central issue less about the commercial appeal of screen production than about the activity’s defined institutional setting: it is production managed by government on a remunerated basis.

Its scope is broad within that setting. It covers the making of moving images, including films, videos and audiovisual works such as 2D animation, 3D animation, stop-motion animation and combinations of animation techniques. It also includes television programmes, television commercials, television news programmes, vlogs and video podcasts. Government-managed sports-media content made as film, video or television programming belongs within the same activity, as do films made for television exhibition, film-delivery services and film booking-agency services when managed by government.

The classification is open across the stated business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That scale availability should be read precisely. It describes the scales listed for the activity; it does not alter the national foreign-ownership ceiling. A foreign stake is not available under this code, regardless of the scale at which the activity might otherwise be organised. The scope also draws a practical boundary around production itself: duplicating films or reproducing audio or video recordings onto CD, DVD or other physical media from a master copy is outside it, as is animation post-production.

Bali’s record adds an important distinction without softening the result. At the Besar scale, the recorded OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so this activity is not caught by Bali’s island-wide permanent PMA moratorium for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI. Yet the Bali status remains **TERTUTUP**. In other words, the moratorium is not the operative barrier described here; the conclusion for foreign ownership remains unchanged in both the national and Bali entries.
editorial.pullQuote: The moratorium is not the operative barrier described here; foreign ownership remains closed nationally and in Bali.
